title: My Last Duchess: publication and speaker
short: Published in Dramatic Lyrics (1842) as 'Italy'; the speaker is a Renaissance Duke of Ferrara, showing his late wife's portrait to an envoy.
body: The poem first appeared in Dramatic Lyrics (1842) under the heading 'Italy and France. I. Italy'; it took its present title in 1849. The speaker is identified in the original headnote as 'Ferrara', and Louis S. Friedland (1936) showed that Browning probably drew on Alfonso II d'Este, fifth Duke of Ferrara, whose first wife, Lucrezia de' Medici, married him in 1558 while still a young teenager and died in 1561, amid rumours of poison. Alfonso then negotiated to marry Barbara of Austria, daughter of the Emperor Ferdinand I and sister of Ferdinand II, Count of Tyrol. 'Last' means 'most recent' and 'final': the Duke is already arranging the next. The poem is the classic example of the dramatic monologue.

title: couplets that hide themselves
short: Rhymed iambic pentameter couplets, so heavily enjambed that the rhymes are barely heard.
body: The poem is written in twenty-eight heroic couplets, but the sentences run across line-ends ('I call / That piece a wonder') and pause in mid-line, so the rhymes rarely close a unit of sense. The effect is of natural, controlled speech that is nevertheless strictly patterned, a formal image of the Duke himself: courteous on the surface, rigidly in control beneath. Ian Lancashire's RPO commentary analyses how the stresses and verbal habits build the speaker's idiolect.

anchor: Looking as if she were alive
title: as if she were alive
short: Praise of the portrait's lifelikeness, which also reminds us the Duchess is dead; the phrase returns at l. 47.
body: On the surface the Duke compliments the painter: the picture looks alive. But 'as if' insists that she is not. When he repeats 'There she stands / As if alive' (ll. 46-47) right after 'all smiles stopped together', the phrase gains a chilling double meaning: the portrait is the Duchess he prefers, one who smiles only when he draws the curtain. RPO's commentary notes that the murder is never stated, only implied by such phrasing.

title: Frà Pandolf
short: An invented painter; 'Frà' (Brother) makes him a friar, which makes the Duke's jealousy of him absurd.
body: No painter of this name is securely identified, and he is usually taken as Browning's invention; being a friar, he is an unlikely seducer. The title 'Frà' (from frate, brother) was used for members of religious orders, like the real painter Fra Filippo Lippi, whom Browning later made a speaker in 'Fra Lippo Lippi' (1855). That the portrait took a single day ('a day') emphasises the painter's skill, and the Duke stresses that he named him 'by design': he wants the visitor to know the picture is a prized work, and perhaps to raise the subject of the Duchess's blush.

title: the curtain
short: The portrait is kept behind a curtain that only the Duke may draw: control of her image replaces control of her.
body: The parenthesis '(since none puts by / The curtain I have drawn for you, but I)' reveals a jealous ownership of the image. Whereas the living Duchess smiled on everyone, the painted Duchess is shown only when the Duke decides. Robert Langbaum's influential reading of the dramatic monologue uses this poem to show how a reader is drawn into a degree of sympathy with a speaker even while judging him: the Duke's charm and confidence hold us as they hold the envoy.

title: the listener
short: The silent auditor is an envoy of the Count whose daughter the Duke means to marry.
body: We learn who the listener is only at the end (l. 49): the agent of 'the Count your master', sent to negotiate a marriage. RPO identifies him, following Friedland, as presumably Nikolaus Madruz (also spelled Mardruz), who led the Count of Tyrol's entourage in the 1560s. His silence is part of the form: everything we infer comes through the Duke's reactions ('Will't please you sit', 'Will't please you rise?', 'Nay, we'll go / Together down'), which hint that the envoy is uneasy and perhaps tries to leave first.

title: that spot / Of joy
short: The Duchess's blush, which the Duke resents because it could be called up by anyone, not only by him.
body: The 'spot of joy' is a flush of pleasure in her cheek. The Duke imagines the painter's compliments ('Her mantle laps / Over my lady's wrist too much', 'Paint / Must never hope to reproduce the faint / Half-flush that dies along her throat') and condemns her for responding to mere 'courtesy'. A mantle (RPO) is a loose sleeveless cloak. The repeated word 'spot' (ll. 14, 21) carries a faint suggestion of a stain: the Duke turns innocent warmth into a fault.

title: A heart--how shall I say?--too soon made glad
short: The Duke's mock hesitation; the 'fault' he names is that his wife was easily pleased and kind to everyone.
body: The interjection performs delicacy, but the charge it introduces is self-condemning: she was 'too easily impressed', she 'liked whate'er / She looked on'. The Duke's account reads as an excuse for a grievance that is really about his own vanity. The asides, dashes and self-corrections ('Somehow--I know not how') are habits of speech by which Browning lets the speaker expose more than he means to.

title: My favor at her breast
short: A love-token he gave her; she valued it no more than a sunset, a bough of cherries or her white mule.
body: A 'favour' (RPO) is a token of love, such as a ribbon or jewel, worn as a sign of attachment. The catalogue that follows puts the Duke's gift on the same level as natural beauty ('The dropping of the daylight in the West'), a present from 'some officious fool', and her mule. 'Officious' here means over-eager to please, meddlesome, though the older sense of 'dutiful' is also available (OED). The Duke's outrage at this levelling reveals his belief that everything she gave should have been graded by rank.

title: a nine-hundred-years-old name
short: The Duke's pride in his ancient lineage; the Este were far older than the Medici, his wife's family.
body: The House of Este was among the oldest noble houses in Italy, whereas Lucrezia's family, the Medici, had risen from banking and only recently acquired ducal rank (Cosimo I became Duke of Florence in 1537). RPO points out the contrast and observes that the Duke's figure of nine hundred years is an exaggeration. The hyphenated compound turns the name into a possession, a 'gift' that he feels his wife valued no more than 'anybody's gift'.

title: skill / In speech--(which I have not)
short: The Duke denies any skill in speech while speaking with great skill: is he self-deceived or calculating?
body: This disclaimer is central to a long critical debate. B. R. Jerman ('Browning's Witless Duke', PMLA 1957) argued that the Duke blunders, revealing more than he intends to a stranger. Laurence Perrine ('Browning's Shrewd Duke', PMLA 1959) replied that the revelation is deliberate: the Duke is warning the envoy, and through him the Count, what he expects of his next wife. Either way, the false modesty is itself a rhetorical device, and the speech that follows ('Just this / Or that in you disgusts me') is a precise rehearsal of the reproof he refused to give.

title: miss ... exceed the mark; lessoned
short: Archery terms: to fall short of or overshoot the target. 'Lessoned' means taught, with a possible pun on 'lessened'.
body: RPO identifies 'miss' and 'exceed the mark' as terms from archery, overshooting the target. The Duke imagines correcting his wife as one corrects a pupil's aim. 'Lessoned' (instructed) may pun on 'lessened', since such correction would diminish her, and on his own diminution if he had to argue with her: 'nor plainly set / Her wits to yours' imagines her answering back as an equal. 'Forsooth' (in truth) is scornful.

title: I choose / Never to stoop
short: The Duke's governing principle: pride forbids him to lower himself even to correct his wife.
body: 'Stoop' appears three times in a few lines (ll. 34, 42, 43), the key word of the Duke's self-image. To explain his displeasure would be beneath him, so he chooses another course, which the next sentence implies. The phrase is in the present tense ('I choose'), a reminder that this principle still governs him and will govern his next marriage. Perrine reads such statements as a deliberate message to the envoy; Jerman as self-exposure.

title: I gave commands; / Then all smiles stopped together
short: The poem's central ambiguity: did he have her killed? Browning said either death or confinement in a convent.
body: The Duke never says what the commands were. Asked whether they meant she was put to death, Browning is reported to have answered that they were that she should be put to death, 'or he might have had her shut up in a convent' (recorded by Hiram Corson, and summarised by RPO and Wikipedia). Most readers hear murder, reinforced by 'There she stands / As if alive'. The flat, short sentences after the long periods of complaint make the moment chilling; then the Duke turns at once to business ('Will't please you rise?').

title: The Count your master
short: The father of the bride-to-be; historically the Tyrolean court at Innsbruck, with which Alfonso II negotiated his second marriage.
body: RPO presumes the Count to be Ferdinand II, Count of Tyrol, whose court was at Innsbruck; strictly, the bride, Barbara of Austria, was his sister and a daughter of the Emperor Ferdinand I, so the identification is approximate. Browning need not have intended an exact historical match. 'Munificence' (generosity) and 'Is ample warrant that no just pretence / Of mine for dowry will be disallowed' mean: the Count's well-known generosity guarantees that any reasonable dowry I ask will be granted. The Duke negotiates money in the same breath as he disclaims it.

title: his fair daughter's self ... is my object
short: 'Object' means aim or goal, but the poem has shown the Duke treating women as objects of possession.
body: Officially the Duke says he wants the daughter herself, not her dowry: 'object' in the sense of purpose (OED). But after his account of the last Duchess, the word cannot escape its other sense, a thing to be acquired and displayed, like the portrait and the bronze. 'As I avowed / At starting' shows the speech is a stage in a negotiation that began earlier.

title: Nay, we'll go / Together down, sir
short: The envoy seems to try to go ahead; the Duke insists they walk together, an apparent courtesy and a display of control.
body: 'Nay' suggests the envoy has moved to go downstairs first, perhaps from deference, perhaps from discomfort. Etiquette would let the lower-ranking visitor follow; by insisting they go 'together', the Duke is either gracious or unwilling to let the guest escape his talk. RPO's commentary notes how much of the listener's behaviour must be inferred from such small signals. The moment also prepares the final gesture, in which the Duke, still walking, points out one more possession.

title: Neptune taming a sea-horse
short: A bronze of the sea-god taming a sea-horse: an emblem of the Duke's idea of mastery, closing the poem.
body: Neptune, the Roman god of the sea, was often shown with sea-horses (hippocamps) drawing his chariot (RPO). The Duke's closing remark turns from the dead wife to another treasure, and the subject of the bronze, a god subduing a wild creature, glosses his own marriage. No sculptor 'Claus of Innsbruck' is securely identified; Innsbruck links him with the Count's court, so the gift may also hint at the alliance. The final line ends, as the poem began, with possession: 'for me'.
